# Clinical decisions and the translational chain {#sec-b01}



::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance
**Guiding question:** Who will do something differently because of the output?

**For:** medical students, clinical researchers and doctoral candidates who are new to data analysis ·
**Prerequisites:** basic clinical knowledge; no programming experience

**In the course:** [W1 · From clinical case to question](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w1-from-clinical-case-to-question.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b01-case}

Ms K., 84 years old, falls in her kitchen early in the morning. She is a fictional patient. In the emergency
department a hip radiograph is taken 30 minutes after arrival. Four minutes later, image-analysis software marks a
possible femoral neck fracture. The radiologist reports 40 minutes after that, and the orthopaedic team plans surgery
for the next morning. After the operation a nurse screens her for delirium, a physiotherapist gets her walking on
the second postoperative day, and on day 5 a case manager decides whether to apply for geriatric rehabilitation.
Every step produces information. This chapter asks a narrower question: which of these outputs changes what a named person does, and what
happens when the output is wrong or missing?

A second, unrelated case runs alongside. A research group measures tissue oxygenation with hyperspectral imaging
(HSI) in six rats after a standardised soft-tissue injury. They want to know whether the signal justifies a study in
patients.

## Core reading {#sec-b01-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W1 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

### An output is worth the action it changes

A test result, a risk score or a coloured box on an image is not useful in itself. It becomes useful when a person
sees it in time, understands it and does something different from what they would otherwise have done. Fryback and
Thornbury described this as a hierarchy for diagnostic imaging [@fryback1991efficacy]. Level 1 is technical image
quality. Level 2 is diagnostic accuracy, such as sensitivity and specificity. Level 3 asks whether the information
changes the clinician's diagnostic thinking. Level 4 asks whether it changes the management plan, level 5 whether
patients are better off, and level 6 whether the benefit justifies the costs to society. Each level is necessary for
the next, but it does not guarantee it.

For Ms K. this hierarchy is concrete. Suppose the fracture flag is highly accurate (level 2). If the radiologist would
have seen the same fracture 40 minutes later and the surgeon would have planned the same operation, nothing
changes at level 4. The same flag can be valuable in a different setting: at night, when a junior doctor reads the
image alone and might send a patient home with an undisplaced fracture. Accuracy belongs to the software. Decision
value belongs to the software *in a particular pathway*.

### The decision map

The simplest tool for this chapter is a decision map (@tbl-b01-map). Each row is one output in Ms K.'s pathway. The
columns force four answers: who acts, which action changes, in which population the output is meant to be used, and
what happens when the output is wrong or unavailable. The last column, the *fallback*, is often forgotten. It
describes how care continues if the software is switched off, gives no answer or gives a wrong one.

| Output | Who acts differently | Changed action | Population | Harm if wrong | Fallback |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Fracture flag on the hip radiograph | Emergency physician, radiologist | Second look; CT if the radiograph is equivocal | Adults with a fall and hip pain in the emergency department | Missed fracture: delayed surgery. False alarm: extra CT, time | Usual radiologist report |
| Delirium screening score after surgery | Ward nurse | Prevention bundle (orientation, sleep, glasses, hearing aids) | Older inpatients after hip surgery | Missed delirium; time spent on low-risk patients | Daily clinical assessment |
| Predicted need for inpatient rehabilitation on day 5 | Case manager | Early application for geriatric rehabilitation | Inpatients after hip fracture surgery | Wrong placement; delayed discharge | Team discussion on the ward round |
| Gait speed in rehabilitation (m/s) | Physiotherapist | Adjust therapy; discuss discharge home | Patients in geriatric rehabilitation | Discharge too early or too late | Therapist's clinical judgement |
| HSI oxygenation index in the rat model | Research team | Plan the next experiment, or stop | Rats in one injury model, not patients | Wasted animals and funding; premature human study | No clinical use; standard assessment continues |

: Decision map for the fictional patient Ms K. (n = 1, *synthetic* case) and for the preclinical HSI study (n = 6 animals, *synthetic*). Each row names one output, the person who acts on it and the route back to usual care. {#tbl-b01-map}

Three entries need particular care. The **population** is where the output was developed and checked, not where it
might conceivably run. A fracture flag trained on emergency radiographs of adults says little about children or
about follow-up images after surgery. The **action** must be specific. “Better decisions” is not an action;
“request CT before discharge” is. The **fallback** must be a route that already works without the tool, so that a
failure of the software does not become a failure of care.

The map rests on one assumption that is easy to overlook: **the person in the ‘who acts’ column sees the output before
the decision is taken, and has the time, the competence and the authority to act differently.** If any of these
conditions fails, accuracy is irrelevant. The Lab and the Counter-check below test the timing part of this
assumption with a few lines of R.

### From rat to patient: the translational chain

The HSI study looks similar but has a different addressee. Nobody treats a patient on the basis of six rats. The
research team decides whether the signal deserves the next experiment. The output is a reason to formulate a
hypothesis, not a reason to change care.

Between the two lies a chain of evidence. A preclinical signal must first be shown to be robust in animals: random
allocation, blinded assessment and complete reporting, for which the ARRIVE guidelines give a checklist
[@percie2020arrive]. Next comes feasibility in patients, then diagnostic accuracy in the target population, which
STARD-AI helps to report [@sounderajah2025stardai]. Early clinical evaluation of a decision-support tool, with real
users in a real workflow, is the subject of DECIDE-AI [@vasey2022decideai]. Only comparative studies can show that
patients are better off. Each link answers a different question, and none can be skipped by a larger sample at an
earlier link.

The chain often breaks. Van der Worp and colleagues cite a review of animal studies from leading high-impact
journals: about one-third of the studies translated to the level of human randomised trials, and about one-tenth of
the interventions were eventually approved for use in patients (*published*) [@vanderworp2010animal]. The same authors list
typical reasons: weak internal validity (no randomisation, no blinding), limited external validity (young, otherwise
healthy animals versus older patients with several diseases) and selective publication of positive results. Ms K. is
84 and takes several medicines. The rats are young, healthy and injured in a standardised way. That gap is not a flaw
of the rat study. It is the reason why its result is a hypothesis.

### Two teaching datasets that must stay apart

This book uses both cases repeatedly, so their data are kept strictly separate. The **fracture cohort** describes
12 fictional patients (identifiers `P01` to `P12`; Ms K. is `P01`). Its unit of analysis is the patient. The **HSI rat
study** describes six fictional animals (`A1` to `A6`). It has thousands of rows, one per image pixel, but only six
independent units. Mixing the two, or counting pixels as if they were animals, would produce numbers that look
precise and mean nothing. @sec-b03 returns to this.

**Question for the workshop:** Choose one row of @tbl-b01-map. At what time, and on which screen or sheet of paper,
must the output appear so that the named person can still act on it? What would make the row worthless?

## Lab {#sec-b01-lab}

This Lab is the first contact with R. Every line is explained, and the expected output is printed below each
command. You can follow the Lab on paper without running anything. If you want to run it, install R and RStudio
first; [CTTIR Course 1, Week 1 Session 2](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course1_foundations/labs/lab_week1_session2.html)
shows the set-up step by step.

### Step 1: R as a calculator

Text after `#` is a comment; R ignores it. The arrow `<-` stores a value under a name.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
xray_min   <- 30        # radiograph taken, minutes after arrival
flag_min   <- 34        # fracture flag available
report_min <- 74        # radiologist's report available
report_min - flag_min   # how many minutes earlier the flag arrives
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 40
```


:::
:::


The line starting with `#>` is R's answer: the flag is available 40 minutes before the report. The `[1]` only means
“first element of the result”.

### Step 2: a table of Ms K.'s pathway

A table in R is called a *data frame*. Each column is a variable, each row an observation. Here one row is one step
in Ms K.'s pathway.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pathway <- data.frame(
  pid  = "P01",                                     # pseudonymous patient identifier
  step = c("Radiograph and fracture flag", "Surgery", "Delirium screening",
           "First walk, gait test", "Rehabilitation decision", "Transfer to rehabilitation",
           "Gait test in rehabilitation", "Follow-up visit"),
  day  = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 16, 92),               # days since arrival (day 0 = arrival)
  role = c("Emergency department", "Surgery", "Ward nursing", "Physiotherapy",
           "Case management", "Case management", "Physiotherapy", "Outpatient clinic")
)
pathway
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   pid                         step day                 role
#> 1 P01 Radiograph and fracture flag   0 Emergency department
#> 2 P01                      Surgery   1              Surgery
#> 3 P01           Delirium screening   2         Ward nursing
#> 4 P01        First walk, gait test   3        Physiotherapy
#> 5 P01      Rehabilitation decision   5      Case management
#> 6 P01   Transfer to rehabilitation   8      Case management
#> 7 P01  Gait test in rehabilitation  16        Physiotherapy
#> 8 P01              Follow-up visit  92    Outpatient clinic
```


:::
:::


How to read this output:

- The numbers 1 to 8 on the left are row numbers. R adds them; they are not data.
- `pid` repeats the same value in every row. It is the *identifier* (ID) that links these rows to Ms K. in other
  tables. It is a pseudonym, not her name. In @sec-b03 the same ID appears in the gait-speed table.
- `day` has a unit: days since arrival in the emergency department. This starting point is called *time zero*. A
  number without its unit and time zero cannot be checked by anyone else. @sec-b03 counts the same gait tests
  from the day of surgery (day 1 here), so the first test appears there as day 2, not day 3.
- `role` names who acts. It is the column that the decision map is about.

Before we draw anything, R checks two facts about the table. `stopifnot()` stops with an error if a statement is
false, so silence means “all true”.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(nrow(pathway) == 8,                # eight steps
          all(diff(pathway$day) >= 0))       # days never go backwards
```
:::


### Step 3: the first graphic

The package **ggplot2** builds a graphic from three parts: the data, the *mapping* of columns to positions or colours
(`aes()`), and the kind of mark (`geom_point()` for points). `library()` loads the package once per session.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)

pathway$step <- factor(pathway$step, levels = rev(pathway$step))   # keep the order top to bottom
pathway$role <- factor(pathway$role, levels = unique(pathway$role))

ggplot(pathway, aes(x = day, y = step, colour = role, shape = role)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "sqrt", breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 5, 8, 16, 30, 60, 92)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(cdsr_colours[c("blue", "orange", "green", "red", "purple", "grey")])) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18, 8, 4)) +
  labs(x = "Days since arrival (square-root scale)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL,
       caption = "Synthetic case, n = 1 patient.") +
  theme_cdsr() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Pathway of the fictional patient Ms K. (`P01`) from the emergency department to the follow-up visit. Horizontal axis: days since arrival (day 0) on a square-root scale; one point per step, coloured by the role that acts. n = 1 patient, 8 steps; *synthetic* case.](b01-clinical-decision_files/figure-html/fig-b01-pathway-1.png){#fig-b01-pathway fig-alt='Dot chart with eight steps listed from top to bottom: radiograph and fracture flag on day 0, surgery on day 1, delirium screening on day 2, first walk on day 3, rehabilitation decision on day 5, transfer to rehabilitation on day 8, gait test in rehabilitation on day 16 and follow-up on day 92. Points are coloured and shaped by role. The horizontal axis is stretched at the start so that the first days are readable.' width=1050}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="What you should see"}
Eight points, one per row of the table, with the radiograph at the top left (day 0) and the follow-up visit at the
bottom right (day 92). The first few days take up most of the width because the axis is drawn on a square-root scale;
equal distances on the axis are therefore *not* equal numbers of days. Two pairs of points share a colour and shape:
case management (days 5 and 8) and physiotherapy (days 3 and 16). If your figure shows fewer points, a row was lost;
if the steps appear in alphabetical order, the `factor()` line was skipped.
:::

### Step 4: the decision map as data

The map in @tbl-b01-map can be stored as a data frame too. This makes a simple quality check possible: no cell may be
empty, because an empty ‘fallback’ is exactly the gap that causes harm when software fails.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
decision_map <- data.frame(
  output     = c("Fracture flag", "Delirium score", "Rehabilitation prediction", "Gait speed", "HSI index"),
  who_acts   = c("Emergency physician, radiologist", "Ward nurse", "Case manager", "Physiotherapist",
                 "Research team"),
  action     = c("Second look; CT if equivocal", "Prevention bundle", "Early application",
                 "Adjust therapy", "Plan or stop next experiment"),
  population = c("Adults, fall, hip pain, ED", "Older inpatients after hip surgery",
                 "Inpatients after hip surgery", "Patients in geriatric rehabilitation", "Rats, one injury model"),
  fallback   = c("Usual report", "Daily assessment", "Ward-round discussion", "Clinical judgement",
                 "No clinical use")
)
stopifnot(all(nzchar(as.matrix(decision_map))))   # nzchar = "not an empty string"
table(clinical = decision_map$population != "Rats, one injury model")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> clinical
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>     1     4
```


:::
:::


Four outputs concern patients and one concerns animals. The `table()` output counts them.

### Step 5: two datasets, two units

The last step builds only the *design* of the two teaching datasets, without measured values, to show the
difference between rows and independent units. `expand.grid()` creates every combination of its arguments.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cohort_design <- expand.grid(window = c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4", "V5"),   # five planned visits
                             pid = sprintf("P%02d", 1:12))                # P01 ... P12
hsi_design <- expand.grid(pixel = 1:200, image = 1:2, limb = c("control", "injured"),
                          animal = sprintf("A%d", 1:6))                   # A1 ... A6

units <- data.frame(
  dataset           = c("Fracture cohort (clinical)", "HSI rat study (preclinical)"),
  rows              = c(nrow(cohort_design), nrow(hsi_design)),
  independent_units = c(length(unique(cohort_design$pid)), length(unique(hsi_design$animal))),
  unit              = c("patient", "animal")
)
units
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                       dataset rows independent_units    unit
#> 1  Fracture cohort (clinical)   60                12 patient
#> 2 HSI rat study (preclinical) 4800                 6  animal
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(units$rows == c(60, 4800), units$independent_units == c(12, 6),
          length(intersect(cohort_design$pid, hsi_design$animal)) == 0)   # no shared IDs
```
:::


The cohort has 60 rows for 12 patients; the rat study has 4,800 rows for six animals. The last check confirms that no
identifier occurs in both datasets, so they cannot be merged by accident.

## Counter-check {#sec-b01-countercheck}

The key assumption of the decision map was timing. Suppose the hospital decides to run the fracture software as a
nightly batch to save computing costs, so that the flag for Ms K. appears 18 hours after arrival instead of after
34 minutes. **Before you run the code, predict:** how many of the four emergency-department decisions below can the
flag still influence?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ed_decisions <- data.frame(
  decision = c("Radiologist's report", "CT if radiograph equivocal", "Plan surgery", "Anaesthesia assessment"),
  hour     = c(74, 80, 120, 150) / 60                # hours since arrival
)
flag_hour_now   <- 34 / 60                           # flag after 34 minutes
flag_hour_batch <- 18                                # nightly batch: 18 hours

ed_decisions$flag_in_time_now   <- flag_hour_now   < ed_decisions$hour
ed_decisions$flag_in_time_batch <- flag_hour_batch < ed_decisions$hour
ed_decisions
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                     decision     hour flag_in_time_now flag_in_time_batch
#> 1       Radiologist's report 1.233333             TRUE              FALSE
#> 2 CT if radiograph equivocal 1.333333             TRUE              FALSE
#> 3               Plan surgery 2.000000             TRUE              FALSE
#> 4     Anaesthesia assessment 2.500000             TRUE              FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(sum(ed_decisions$flag_in_time_now) == 4, sum(ed_decisions$flag_in_time_batch) == 0)
```
:::


With immediate processing the flag precedes all four decisions; as a nightly batch it precedes none. Its sensitivity
and specificity are unchanged, yet its decision value for Ms K. falls to zero. The same logic applies to every row of
@tbl-b01-map: a delirium score that appears after the ward round, or a rehabilitation prediction delivered after the
application deadline, cannot change the action it was built for.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b01-consequences}

**Patients.** A missed fracture means pain, a second visit and delayed surgery; a false alarm means an extra CT, more
radiation and more time in the emergency department. Both errors fall on the patient, but they are not equal, and the
decision map makes the trade-off visible before any accuracy figure is discussed. @sec-b09 turns these errors into
counts per shift, and @sec-b21 asks who carries them.

**Operations.** Every output needs a named owner and a fallback that works without it. If the fracture software fails
at 3 a.m., the radiologist's report remains the basis of care. A tool whose failure goes unnoticed is more dangerous
than no tool, because staff may rely on a silence that only means “not processed”. Monitoring and stopping rules are
the subject of @sec-b20.

**Regulation.** Whether fracture-flagging software is a medical device depends on its intended purpose, as set by the
manufacturer, under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR, Regulation (EU) 2017/745) [@eu2017mdr]. Annex VIII,
Rule 11 of this binding text classifies software that provides information used for diagnostic or therapeutic
decisions. In which class a given product falls, and which obligations of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
(Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) apply from which date [@eu2024aiact;
@eu2026omnibus], is worked through in @sec-b22 (status: November 2026). A research prototype that is quietly used for patient care
changes its regulatory position; that is a question for the institution, not for the analyst alone (*open*, to be
clarified locally with the regulatory affairs or medical device officer).

**Animal research.** The rat study is subject to Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for
scientific purposes [@eu2010animals], published on 20 October 2010 and in force since 9 November 2010. Its Article 4
obliges Member States to ensure replacement, reduction and refinement (the 3Rs) wherever possible; the national
implementing provisions apply from 1 January 2013. Which national authority approves a given project is a local
question (*open*, to be clarified with the institution's animal welfare body). ARRIVE 2.0
governs how the study is reported [@percie2020arrive], and the NC3Rs explain the 3Rs for planning [@nc3rs3rs]. A
within-animal control limb, as in our design, is one way to reduce animal numbers, but it does not replace a
justified sample size (@sec-b16).

**Data protection.** Not directly touched here, because all data are *synthetic*. It becomes relevant as soon as real
radiographs or registry data leave the treating hospital (@sec-b23).

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b01-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** For the output you evaluate, which named role changes which action, at what time after time
  zero, in which population — and what is the fallback when the output is missing or wrong?
- **Self-test:** A model predicts on day 7 after hip surgery whether a patient will need inpatient rehabilitation. In
  the hospital, rehabilitation applications must be submitted by day 5. The model's discrimination is good. What is its
  decision value in this pathway, and what would you change first: the model, its timing or its addressee?

  ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
  As deployed, the decision value is zero: the output arrives after the decision it is meant to inform. Improving the
  model's accuracy does not help. The first change is the timing (predict on day 3 or 4 with the information then
  available, which may lower accuracy) or the addressee (use the prediction for a later decision, such as the timing
  of discharge from rehabilitation). Fryback and Thornbury's levels 3 and 4 are not reached, whatever level 2 shows.
  :::

- **Annotated sources:**

    from decision value in this chapter.
  - @vanderworp2010animal — reasons why animal findings fail to translate, with the published estimate quoted in the
    Core reading.
  - @percie2020arrive — ARRIVE 2.0, the reporting checklist for the rat study.
  - @sounderajah2025stardai — STARD-AI, reporting of diagnostic accuracy studies of AI tools (level 2).
  - @vasey2022decideai — DECIDE-AI, reporting of early clinical evaluation in real workflows (levels 3 and 4).
  - @eu2010animals — the binding EU basis for the 3Rs (Article 4).
